## 2.1 Data sources and construction

This study uses farm-level data from the three most recent Ghana Living Standards Surveys: GLSS5, conducted in 2005/06; GLSS6, conducted in 2012/13; and GLSS7, conducted in 2016/17. The GLSS surveys are repeated cross-sectional household surveys that use a two-stage sampling design, with enumeration areas selected in the first stage and households selected in the second stage. We rely on the consolidated farmer-level GLSS dataset developed by (Tsiboe 2020), which harmonizes farm production outcomes across survey rounds and has been used to study agricultural productivity across multiple Ghanaian crop value chains (Tsiboe et al. 2019, 2021a, 2021b, 2022; Tsiboe 2021). All monetary values are expressed in constant 2016/17 Ghana cedis using the national consumer price index. [[WIRE: state whether survey weights are applied to the descriptive statistics and, if so, which weight variable — `WeightHH` is carried in the analysis file. resource_extraction states this explicitly; land_tenure's omission is flagged as a defect in its own source file, and should not be inherited.]]

Although the consolidated dataset provides harmonized farm-level outcomes, it does not directly contain the community-level agricultural service provision indicators required for this study. To construct these measures, we returned to the agriculture section of the GLSS **community** questionnaire, which records the service environment of the enumeration area rather than of any individual household, and merged it into the farmer-level data using survey and enumeration-area identifiers. The community questionnaire is administered not to households but to a panel of community opinion leaders, and the survey protocol requires that panel to reflect the occupational, ethnic, gender, and religious composition of the community. Our treatment measures are therefore key-informant reports of what is *available* in a locality, not administrative records and not household reports of services *received*. That distinction governs how the estimates should be read, and we return to it below.

Community agricultural service variables are harmonized using GLSS7 as the reference structure, since it is the most recent round and organizes the service questions most clearly. In GLSS7 the relevant items are cs5q5--cs5q15, covering the presence and distance of an agricultural extension office, whether an extension officer is stationed in the community, whether an officer visits farmers, the provider agency, the services extension agents provide, compliance with extension guidance, the presence of an agricultural or fishing association, the services that association provides, cooperative participation, and tractor availability. GLSS6 is numbered identically to GLSS7 across this block. GLSS5 requires renaming, because it lacks the compliance item and its association, cooperative, and tractor questions therefore sit one position earlier than in the later rounds. Where a community contributes more than one record, indicators are collapsed to one observation per survey and enumeration area by taking the maximum, so a service counts as available if any informant record reports it. Appendix Table S1 gives the source question and construction rule for every variable; Table S2 documents the cross-round mapping. **Compliance with extension guidance is not available in GLSS5**, and every statistic involving it is therefore restricted to GLSS6 and GLSS7.

For the meta-stochastic frontier analysis we define four indicators of the institutional source of service delivery. A community is classified as having: (i) *any service source* if it has an agricultural or fishing association, an agricultural cooperative, or active extension; (ii) an *association* source if an agricultural or fishing association is present; (iii) a *cooperative* source if farmers participate in an agricultural cooperative; and (iv) an *active extension* source if an extension officer visits farmers in the community. These are four separate binary treatments, each estimated against its own pair of group-specific frontiers, rather than four levels of a single categorical treatment. A second set of indicators captures the *content* of services available — planting or seed-use support, mechanization, credit, irrigation, animal husbandry, fertilizer and other agrochemical inputs, and post-harvest, marketing or storage support — and enters the analysis as covariates rather than as treatments. [[WIRE: the content indicators for credit, mechanization, agrochemicals and post-harvest draw on both the extension-service roster and the association-service roster, so they measure availability from either provider. Confirm this is the intended reading before the sentence above is finalized; see narrative/diagnostics/ag_services_harmonization_audit_plan.md §1.5.]]

Active extension requires a threshold, because the underlying variable is not binary. The community questionnaire asks separately whether an extension office exists, whether an officer is stationed locally, and whether an officer visits farmers, and the harmonized variable combines the three into seven states running from no extension presence at all to office, stationed officer, and visits together. We classify a community as having active extension when an officer visits, which is precisely the partition above which farmer-facing contact occurs. The reason is the object the frontier estimates: a frontier characterises a technology a farmer can actually reach, and an extension office in a community no officer visits does not place a farmer on a different technology from one with no office at all. The alternative rule — counting any extension infrastructure — would pool communities with farmer contact and communities with only a building. The choice is not close-run: [[WIRE: prevalence of active extension at the visit threshold versus at any-infrastructure, by round, from the descriptive exhibits; the draft's Table 3 puts visits at roughly 0.32 pooled against 0.02 for officer-only and 0.03 for office-only.]] Two features of the underlying variable should be noted. Its lower states are not ordered by intensity — an office without an officer and an officer without an office are two kinds of passive presence, not two rungs of a ladder — so the rule is a partition rather than a dose threshold. And communities with an office or a stationed officer but no visits are classified as having no active extension; Section [[WIRE: results section number]] reports the estimates under a stricter definition that also excludes them from the comparison group.

The comparison group for the three source-specific treatments requires one further rule, and it departs from the siblings. A community that has no association but does have a cooperative or active extension is set to missing rather than to zero, and so drops out of the association comparison entirely; the same applies to the cooperative and active-extension contrasts. The reason is that such a community is *treated under a different arm*, not untreated: coding it zero would place served farms in the reference group and contaminate the frontier the treated group is measured against, rather than merely mislabelling a category. The retained comparison group is therefore communities with no agricultural service source of any kind. We do not claim that this estimates the effect of an association relative to other service arrangements; we claim it estimates the difference between association-served communities and communities with no service source at all. [[WIRE: count and share excluded under each of the three rules, and a comparison of excluded units against retained controls on the matching covariates.]] Because all four contrasts retain the same comparison group, their estimates are not statistically independent and should not be pooled or differenced as if drawn from separate samples. Section [[WIRE: results section number]] reports a robustness arm in which excluded communities are coded zero instead.

Under these definitions, [[WIRE: prevalence of each of the four treatments, by round and pooled, from the descriptive exhibits.]] Unless otherwise stated, terms such as *"association community"* or *"community with active extension"* in this paper refer to this community-level classification. Every sampled farmer residing in a classified enumeration area is treated as exposed, regardless of whether that farmer personally received a service, belonged to the association, or met an extension officer. This is the paper's central interpretive commitment: the estimates describe the effect of operating in a service-provisioned locality, not of individual programme participation, and they will understate the difference between participants and non-participants to the extent that provision and uptake diverge.

Three features of the instrument bound what these measures can support. Service provision is reported by community informants, so the treatment records availability rather than receipt, and a community counted as served may contain farmers who never used the service. The service-content items are asked only where a provider exists, so their absence for unserved communities is assigned by construction rather than measured, and content contrasts compare a measured category against a definitional one — the only design the questionnaire's skip pattern permits. And implausible values are set to missing: extension distances of 999 kilometres or more, and tractor counts of 99 or more, are treated as non-responses rather than as observations. [[WIRE: number of records affected by each rule, by round — this has never been reported anywhere.]]

The analysis is restricted to crop farmers with reported yields, measured in kilograms per hectare, between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles within each survey round and crop. The final sample includes [[WIRE: final N after the corrected harmonization; the draft reports 22,519 against the pre-audit release]] farm operators cultivating at least one of the following crops: banana, beans, cashew, cassava, citrus fruits, cocoa, coconut, cocoyam, cotton, kenaf, maize, millet, oil palm, peanuts, plantain, potato, rice, sorghum, yam, sugarcane, tomato, pepper, okra, onion, eggplant, and other reported crops.
